If it really was a broad historical phenomenon, then its meaning and influence must have extended beyond those particular people.

It may have appeared under the name of the “Book of Luqmān” or the “wisdom of Luqmān,” just as it appeared under the names “Ḥunafāʾ” and “Aḥnāf.” It may also have appeared under other names that we have not yet discovered.
It may likewise have expressed itself in different forms: speeches, poetry, or sayings of wisdom that circulated like proverbs.

And beyond all of this, its meaning and historical direction found their fullest expression in Islam itself, as the report from Ibn al-Athīr suggests through the words attributed to the founder of Islam.
If this phenomenon had developed so widely and had become so historically important, how did it leave its own period behind in such a “vague and blurred” form?
But the question demands continued investigation, just as scholars have continued to search for the answer to the problem of the “missing link” in the history of human evolution.

What we have seen so far shows that the religious phenomena of Arab society shortly before Islam reflected the particular historical relationship between pre-Islamic social reality and pre-Islamic social consciousness.
But in the phenomenon of the Ḥunafāʾ they also reflected a sign of historical change within religious consciousness itself.
In its real historical meaning, this change in religious consciousness was an almost direct expression of the transformation taking place in the material foundations of the old tribal system.

That system had reached a point where social conflict was beginning to emerge from within it. Differences in wealth and social position were widening inside individual tribes and across pre-Islamic society as a whole.

Seen in this way, the appearance of Islam within this society was clearly not a sudden event that descended upon it without any previous connection to the historical conditions already developing there.
The Islamic mission appeared specifically in Meccan society, where social conflicts had become sharper than in any other part of the peninsula.
This itself shows that Islam did not arise in a vacuum.

It arose because the objective conditions of pre-Islamic society had developed in a way that called for something new. The economic, social, and intellectual development of Arab society had reached a point at which Islam could emerge from that existing reality in its new form.
The Qur’an, as the central phenomenon of Islam, supports this analysis.
Throughout its surahs, especially those from the Meccan period, we find concrete images of all the phenomena described in this chapter.
Some appear through symbols and suggestion. Some take the form of concentrated or more extended instruction. Others appear as warnings of punishment in the next life or promises of reward.
We can therefore say that the religious phenomena discussed above were reflected in the Qur’an just as the other features of pre-Islamic Arab society were reflected in it.

We will now read several Qur’anic passages that give a direct picture of the different religions, tendencies, and beliefs found among the people of pre-Islamic Arabia in different parts of the peninsula.
Verses that mention Jews, Christians, Sabians, and Zoroastrians on the one hand, and those who associated other beings with God in worship on the other:

Those who believe, those who are Jews, the Sabians, the Christians, the Zoroastrians, and those who associate others with God—God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. (Surat al-Ḥajj, 22:17)
Verses that speak about the Dahriyya, meaning those who denied divine creation of the universe and resurrection after death:

They say, “There is nothing but this worldly life of ours. We die and we live, and nothing destroys us except time.” But they have no knowledge of this. They are only guessing. (Surat al-Jāthiya, 45:24)
Verses about people who accepted a Creator and believed that the world had been brought into existence, but denied resurrection and the return of the body after death:

He gives Us an example and forgets his own creation. He says, “Who will bring these bones back to life after they have decayed?” Say, “The One who created them the first time will bring them back to life, and He has full knowledge of every creation.” (Surat Yā Sīn, 36:78–79)

Verses about people who accepted divine creation and resurrection but rejected prophecy and worshipped idols on the grounds that these idols would act as intermediaries between them and God. Some of these people made pilgrimage to the idols at the Kaaba:

True religion belongs to God alone. As for those who take protectors besides Him, saying, “We worship them only so that they may bring us closer to God,” God will judge between them concerning what they disagree about. (Surat al-Zumar, 39:3)
Through passages like these, Islam itself shows how closely connected it was to the historical transformation discussed throughout this chapter.

That transformation was the process by which pre-Islamic Arab society was undergoing changes in the material foundations of its tribal system. One result of those changes was a shift in the way people understood the world.
Can we now say that we have succeeded in outlining the main features of one stage in the history of Arab thought—a stage that stands at the beginning of the history we are trying to trace?
We call it a “beginning,” but not in the literal historical sense.
It was certainly not the first stage in the actual development of Arab thought.

It is only the earliest stage available to us because the stages that came before it have so far disappeared completely from the written, archaeological, and epigraphic record of Arab history, for reasons that have not yet been discovered.
From this chapter, we can draw several main conclusions about the level of social development in pre-Islamic society.
First: We have seen that the Arabs of the Arabian Peninsula before Islam were not isolated from the outside world.
Their geographical position in the middle of the civilized world of antiquity and the Middle Ages helped prevent such isolation.

The peninsula became an international bridge for trade. Through it, the peoples of East and West, Asia and Africa, exchanged natural and manufactured goods. Social, political, and cultural influences also moved back and forth across it.

Second: The great trade routes running through the peninsula from south to north and north to south created both material and cultural contact between the Arabs and peoples, communities, and states outside Arabia.
By the end of the sixth century CE, these contacts helped create the objective conditions for the breakdown of the primitive tribal system and its distinctive social structure.
At the same time, the first signs appeared of a new and more developed social order that could eventually replace the old nomadic tribal structure.
That old structure had already begun to weaken under the pressure of growing economic and social differences.
These differences appeared in nomadic areas, in settled and semi-settled farming regions, and especially in towns.

They were beginning to prepare the way for a new form of social division that would later develop into class division: first between the rich and poor within the tribe, and then between those who owned the means of production and those who did not.
Third: This social development had not yet matured enough to produce a state among the pre-Islamic Arabs.
But it had already produced the first seed of a state in Meccan society, which at the time was more developed than Arab society elsewhere in the peninsula.
This was mainly because trade and commercial wealth had become concentrated in Mecca, where private ownership was also becoming more clearly defined.

These developments led the wealthy leaders of Quraysh to organize themselves in order to protect their interests and regulate their material relations with other groups in Mecca and with the inhabitants of the peninsula more generally.
From this emerged an early political organization known historically as Dār al-Nadwa.
Arab historians have compared it with the council of elders in Athens, who gathered in the assembly known as the Ekklesia to discuss public affairs.
This social development was clearly reflected in the different forms of culture that could arise in a society living under such historical conditions.
These forms of culture, however, did not all develop to the same degree, and they did not all reflect social reality in the same way.
The first chapter allows us to draw the following broad conclusions.
First: Poetry and language were more highly developed than the other forms of culture found in pre-Islamic society.
This suggests that both had deeper roots in the peninsula’s older history, when parts of Arabia had reached a relatively high level of development.

The clearest evidence comes from the south of the peninsula, especially Yemen, where historically known states such as Sabaʾ, Maʿīn, and Ḥimyar had developed advanced forms of civilization going back to the period before the Common Era.
For reasons that historians have still not been able to explain with confidence, a historical break occurred between that ancient past and the pre-Islamic society of the sixth century CE.
This break cast a long shadow over the economic and social conditions of the sixth century, which appeared in much less developed forms.
Yet poetry and language do not reflect that decline in the same way.
These two parts of pre-Islamic culture had developed far beyond the other areas of life around them.
Second: Pre-Islamic knowledge consisted mainly of scattered and unsystematic results drawn from direct sensory experience and simple forms of reasoning.
Such knowledge developed through everyday contact with nature and with the cosmic phenomena visible to people and directly affecting their lives.
It also developed through the particular social relations in which people lived.
Those relations produced specific customs, traditions, and customary legal practices that served among them much the same purpose that formal laws served in more developed societies.
Third: Of all the forms of consciousness found in pre-Islamic society, religion was the most strongly affected by changes in people’s material life.
As long as the primitive tribal system remained dominant, dividing society into tribal communities based on blood and kinship in their narrowest form, paganism remained the dominant religion.
This was because paganism reflected, in religious consciousness, the structure of the tribal world itself.
The human world was divided into many small and fragmented communities, and pagan religion reflected that same pattern.
It did so in two ways.
First, paganism gave a simple and early form to the relationship between human beings and the natural forces and phenomena that directly affected their daily lives.
It presented those forces as holding absolute, fixed, and unavoidable power over human beings.
Second, paganism rested on a multiplicity of gods that reflected the multiplicity of separate tribal communities.
But shortly before Islam, pre-Islamic society began to undergo changes in its social structure.
Its social relations were starting to move toward a new form of division, one that was preparing the ground for class division.
Religious life began to respond to this wider social transformation.
A movement toward belief in one God now became visible.
It appeared first in Jewish monotheism, which established a base for Judaism in certain regions.
It appeared second in the Christian form of monotheism, which established a base for Christianity in other regions.
Then, toward the end of the pre-Islamic period, a new religious form emerged.
It did not adopt the Jewish or Christian understanding of one God. Instead, it moved toward the understanding of monotheism that would later become Islamic.
This was the religion of the Ḥunafāʾ.
At the level of religious consciousness, it was the clearest expression of pre-Islamic Arab society’s growing conflict with its old, fragmented, and plural tribal system.
